name: Derbforgaill
sources: Hull, Eleanor. The Cuchullin Saga in Irish Literature. (London: David Nutt, 1898), 82.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Derbforgaill (also Dervorgilla or Devorgilla) was a name borne by several Irish heroines. One Derbforgaill of Leinster was a real woman of the 12th century. She married Ua Ruairc, the O'Rourke chieftain of Breffni near Sligo. While her husband was on pilgrimage, she ran off with, or was taken by, Diarmait mac Murchada, also called Dermot MacMurrough. The war between husband and lover drew Norman warriors into Ireland. Their coming destroyed the old Celtic way of life. England later used that breach as its claim to Ireland. History derides her as an adulteress. She acted on the ancient Irish belief that a woman held the right to choose her own consort. A second Derbforgaill belonged to myth. She was the shape-shifting daughter of king Ruad. She conceived a passion for Cúchulainn. She and her maidens turned into swans to fly to him. Cúchulainn threw stones and brought her to earth. He fell to his knees and sucked the stone from her flesh. That act made them blood kin. It thwarted her wish to share his bed. She married his friend Lugaidh Riab nDerg. She died when other women, enraged in a contest, fell upon her. Cúchulainn avenged her by killing 150 women.
objective: This entry records Derbforgaill, a name shared by women of Leinster history and Irish myth.
